name: immortality

attributes.attribute: a concept of never suffering death, unclear in the Celtic vision of divinity
tied to magical food such as the pigs of Manannán Mac Lir and cauldron of Goibniu

sources: Evans-Wentz, W. Y. The Fairy-Faith in Celtic Countries. Gerrards Cross: Colin Smythe Humanities Press, 1911, 503.
MacCulloch, J. A. The Religion of the Ancient Celts. London: Constable, 1911.
Monaghan, Patricia. The Encyclopedia of Celtic Mythology and Folklore. Checkmark Books, 2008.
text: Immortality is a Celtic cosmological concept. Some writers call the Celtic gods immortal. Yet the tales of the battles of Mag Tuired describe the deaths of many gods. Some gods and goddesses were victims of treacherous murder. The queen Medb was struck down while bathing. It is not clear that the idea of never suffering death was part of the Celtic vision of divinity. Some Irish legends speak of magical food. It kept the gods young and healthy. Such food was the pigs of the sea god Manannán Mac Lir, the contents of the ever-full cauldron of the smith Goibniu, and apples from the Otherworld. Without such food, the gods might age and die like mortals. Some ancient sources speak of a Celtic belief in the immortality of the soul.

okr.objective: Document the Celtic cosmological concept of immortality.
key_results: Record the deaths of gods in the tales of Mag Tuired.
Note the magical food that kept gods young.
Note the ancient belief in the immortality of the soul.
